prompt: A stable service keeps about 30 database connections busy on average. Why is configuring exactly 30 connections without further measurement risky?

options.text: A larger pool always improves the database's throughput
options.explanation: Incorrect. Excess connections can add contention and overhead; database capacity still limits useful concurrency.

options.text: Average occupancy already includes the worst burst
options.explanation: Incorrect. An average does not describe peak or tail occupancy.

options.text: Bursts and variable holding times can exhaust the pool; test headroom against database capacity
options.explanation: Correct. Little's law relates averages and does not supply a safe pool maximum by itself.

options.text: Only total HTTP duration matters, even if connections are released much earlier
options.explanation: Incorrect. Connection sizing uses the time the connection is held, rather than unrelated request work.

workedExample: Use Little's law to estimate average resource occupancy, then separate it from a capacity decision. Measure bursts, latency tails and how long connections are held. Check the total across all app instances against what the database can sustain before choosing headroom.

prompt: A service uses one thread per request. A downstream dependency becomes much slower while arrivals stay unchanged, and the caller's fixed-size thread pools had only modest spare capacity. What is the likely failure mechanism?

options.text: Nothing changes because incoming traffic has not increased
options.explanation: Incorrect. Longer request-holding time increases the concurrency needed at the same throughput.

options.text: The service autoscales out of trouble immediately
options.explanation: Incorrect. Autoscaling may not react quickly enough, and extra instances add more load to the already-degraded dependency. Timeouts, circuit breakers and bulkheads are the proper defence.

options.text: Threads are released immediately whenever the dependency is slow
options.explanation: Incorrect. In this blocking design, a request occupies its thread while waiting.

options.text: More threads remain occupied, pools fill, and excess requests queue or fail
options.explanation: Correct. Resource holding time increased without an equivalent increase in capacity, so the caller can exhaust its pools.

workedExample: Follow a thread: it remains occupied until its slow call finishes or times out. At unchanged arrivals, longer occupancy requires more threads to maintain throughput. Once the pool fills, further work waits or is rejected; the old throughput cannot simply be assumed stable. Bound waiting, set appropriate timeouts, isolate dependency pools and shed load. Extra callers can worsen the downstream overload.
